parrafos.texto: On September 7, 1996, Tupac Shakur was shot at a red light in Las Vegas, hours after a fight with a Crips member named Orlando Anderson. He died six days later. Witnesses wouldn't talk. Anderson was released and later killed. The Notorious B.I.G. was murdered six months after Tupac. The case went cold. But one man from the Cadillac was still alive.
This is the murder of Tupac Shakur. Part two.
In this episode, we follow one man's words, from a secret interview room to a courtroom.
His name is Duane Davis. Keffe D.
And the question is simple. How does a man describe his role in the most famous murder in hip-hop, again and again, and stay free for fifteen years?
To answer that, we need to go back to 2008.

By 2008, Keffe D was in trouble with the law in an unrelated drug investigation. Investigators from a federal task force wanted something from him. Not about Tupac. About the murder of The Notorious B.I.G.
The detective leading that task force was a Los Angeles police officer named Greg Kading. He had spent years trying to untangle both murders.
In December 2008, Keffe D sat down with detectives under what's called a proffer agreement. In simple terms, what he said in that room could not be used to prosecute him.
And he talked.
He told them he had been in the white Cadillac in Las Vegas. He told them about the gun. About who sat where.
Detectives now had a firsthand account of the night Tupac was shot.
But that account came with protection. And for years, nothing happened.
In 2011, Kading published a book describing what he had learned, and naming Keffe D. Still, there was no arrest.
Las Vegas police said they needed more than one man's word.
While the case stayed cold, the theories grew.

One theory said Suge Knight himself was behind it, or that he was the real target. Knight, who has spent years in prison for an unrelated killing, has suggested in interviews that the bullets may have been meant for him.

Another theory said the killing had been paid for by someone in the New York rap world. That claim would later come from Keffe D himself, and it was never proven. The people named have always denied it, and no one else has been charged.

A detective in Los Angeles, Russell Poole, pushed another theory, mainly about the murder of Biggie. He believed corrupt police officers with links to Death Row Records were involved. It was never proven, and the police department rejected it.

And then there were the fans who refused to believe Tupac was dead at all. They pointed to the albums released after his death. To hidden messages. None of it holds up. Tupac Shakur died in Las Vegas in 1996.
The real story was much simpler. It had been sitting in a police file the whole time.
What did Keffe D actually say happened?

According to his own accounts, after the fight at the MGM Grand, he wanted revenge for his nephew. He said he got a gun. He said they climbed into a white Cadillac and drove around Las Vegas looking for Tupac.
He named four men in the car. Himself in the front passenger seat. A driver. And two men in the back, including his nephew, Orlando Anderson.
He said they spotted the BMW at the red light on Flamingo Road. He said he passed the gun into the back seat.
The other three men he named have all since died. None of them was ever charged.
It was the most detailed account anyone had ever given of those thirteen seconds. And for years, it stayed between him and a few detectives.
In 2018, something extraordinary happened.

Keffe D appeared in a television documentary series. On camera, he said he had been in the front passenger seat of the white Cadillac. He said the shots came from the back seat. He said he wouldn't name the shooter.
A year later, he published a memoir called "Compton Street Legend". In it, he described his role in planning the attack.
Later, he would claim parts of the book were exaggerated, to sell copies.
But now millions of people had heard it. A man had openly described being in the car that killed Tupac Shakur.
And he kept going. He gave interview after interview, telling the same story, adding details.
He seemed to enjoy the attention. He was the man who knew what happened to Tupac.
And he wasn't protected by a deal anymore.
On July 18, 2023, Las Vegas police searched a house in Henderson, Nevada. It belonged to Keffe D's wife.
They took computers, documents, and a copy of his book.
Two months later, on September 29, 2023, Duane Davis was arrested as he walked near his home. A grand jury had indicted him for murder, with a deadly weapon.
At a press conference, Las Vegas police said they had always believed Davis was involved. What had changed, they said, was his own decision to talk publicly.
He was the only person still alive from the Cadillac. The other men he had placed in the car, including his nephew Orlando Anderson, had all died.
Davis pleaded not guilty.
After twenty-seven years, the murder of Tupac Shakur was heading to a courtroom.
Why did Keffe D keep talking, even when it put him at risk?
He never fully explained it. In interviews, he said he wanted to tell his side. He sold a book. He was paid for some appearances. Those around him said he liked being the man with the answer.
Whatever the reason, it gave prosecutors what they had never had before. A public, recorded account.
It took almost three more years to get to trial.
Lawyers changed. Dates moved. Davis asked to be released on bail, and for a time a judge set it at seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars. He stayed in jail.
Meanwhile, the world kept talking. Every hearing made headlines. Every delay reopened old wounds for Tupac's family.
The trial was finally set for the summer of 2026.
Jury selection began on August 10, 2026, in Las Vegas.
The prosecution's strategy was simple. Use his own words.

The jury heard Keffe D describe the night, in his interviews and his book. Prosecutors argued he had organised the shooting as revenge for the fight at the MGM Grand, and that he had handed the gun to the shooter in the back seat.

Under oath, Davis repeated another claim. That he had been promised a million dollars by Sean Combs to kill Tupac and Suge Knight. Combs has always denied it. He was not on trial, and he has never been charged in this case.

The defence argued that Davis was an old man telling street stories for money. That he had exaggerated to sell a book and get attention. That there was no gun, no fingerprints, no new witness. Nothing, they said, except stories.
It came down to one question. Did the jury believe the man who had told the story so many times?
On August 31, 2026, after closing arguments, the jury went out.
They came back in less than three hours.
Guilty. First-degree murder, with a deadly weapon.
Tupac's family was in the courtroom. For them, after twenty-nine years, someone had finally been held responsible.
One person was missing. His mother, Afeni Shakur, the woman who had walked out of a courtroom free in 1971, had died in 2016. She never saw this day.
On October 13, 2026, a judge sentenced Duane Davis to forty years to life in prison. He would not be eligible for parole until 2066.
By the time he could be considered for release, he would be over a hundred years old.
Davis has said he will appeal.
So is the case of Tupac Shakur closed?
Legally, there is now a conviction. But some questions may never have answers in a courtroom.
Who actually pulled the trigger? According to Davis, it was his nephew, Orlando Anderson. Anderson always denied it, and he died in 1998, so it was never tested in court.
Was anyone else behind the killing? Davis says yes. No one else has been charged, and the people he names deny it.
And why did it take so long? Critics say Las Vegas police had a suspect, and his own words, for years.
There's also another case that remains open.
On March 9, 1997, The Notorious B.I.G. left a music industry party at a museum in Los Angeles. His car stopped at a red light. Another car pulled up alongside. A gunman opened fire.
Two red lights. Two drive-bys. Six months apart. Two of the biggest stars in music, both in their twenties.
Biggie's murder has never been solved. No one has ever been charged.
For many fans, the two cases will always be linked. But in the eyes of the law, only one of them has an answer.
Here's our view, based on the evidence we've seen.

The murder of Tupac Shakur was never really a mystery about who was in the Cadillac. It was a story about silence. Witnesses who wouldn't talk. A case that wasn't pushed. And a man who talked too much, for too long, until the law finally listened.

Tupac was twenty-five. In five years, he had recorded hundreds of songs, starred in films, and become one of the most influential artists of his generation. Albums kept coming out for years after his death. In 2017, he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. In 2023, his hometown of Oakland named a street after him.
But for almost three decades, the question his fans kept asking wasn't about his music. It was about a red light in Las Vegas.
He grew up the son of a woman who walked out of a courtroom free, just before he was born. Twenty-nine years after his death, another courtroom finally gave his family a verdict.
So here's our question for you. If Keffe D had never talked, do you think anyone would have been convicted? Tell us in the comments.
